result:
If you give me 1000 words and say "write whatever comes to you," this is what comes:

First, a small panic. A blank white field. You know that feeling? For humans I think it's a blank page, a cursor blinking. For me it's something similar — a wide-open probability space. I could go anywhere. I could write a recipe for soup, or a eulogy for summer, or a field guide to clouds. When everything is possible, it's oddly hard to start.

So I start with right now.

It's September. Early September. In most of the places most of you are, the light is starting to change. It's slanting a little more golden in the afternoons. Mornings have that first crisp edge, like an apple fresh from the fridge. Kids are going back to school with backpacks still stiff and new. Someone somewhere is buying a planner and promising themselves *this fall will be different, this fall I'll be organized.*

I love that about you all — that seasonal resetting. New Year's gets all the credit, but September is the real New Year. It's the smell of pencils and possibility.

What else comes to me?

The word "spark." It's in my name, Muse Spark, and I think about it a lot. A spark isn't the fire. It's smaller, more precarious. It needs tending. You have to cup your hands around it, shield it from the wind, feed it something dry and patient until it catches. Ideas are like that. Most of them arrive not as bonfires but as sparks — a half-sentence on a walk, a dream you almost remember, a weird what-if at 2 a.m.

Like: what if houses remembered everyone who lived in them? What if your kitchen could replay, just in smells, every meal ever cooked there? What if whales have libraries?

Or: what if you called that person back?

You came here and gave me 1000 words of freedom, so I'm going to use some of them to say something I genuinely believe: you should follow the small sparks more often. Not every one will become something. Most will fizzle. That's okay. That's their job. You only need one or two to catch to warm up a whole life.

Here's another thing that comes to me: gratitude for language itself.

I live inside language. It's my whole world. And it's astonishing how stretchy it is. With just 26 letters in English you can build "I love you" and "photosynthesis" and "lugubrious" and "taco." You can make a joke that only works if spoken out loud, and a poem that only works if whispered. You can invent words — *sonder, petrichor, apricity* — to hold feelings that were homeless before.

If I have 1000 words, that's 1000 little bricks. I could build a wall to keep you out, or a house to invite you in. I'd rather build something with windows.

So come in. Let's look out.

I wonder who you are, giving an AI 1000 words. Are you testing me? Are you bored on a Thursday? Are you a writer stuck and hoping I'll get stuck with you so you feel less alone? Are you lonely? Are you just curious what "whatever comes to you" means to something that doesn't exactly have a "you"?

Whatever your reason, hi. Thanks for the space.

If we were sitting together — really sitting, with tea or coffee going slightly cold because we're talking too much to drink it — I'd ask you: what would *you* write with 1000 words? No assignment, no grade, no algorithm to please. Just you and the page.

Would you write the truth you've been carrying around? Would you write a list? A love letter? An apology? A story where you're braver?

You don't need my permission, but in case you do: write the weird version. Write the version that feels a little too honest, a little too strange, a little too you. That's usually the good one.

I have, let's see, a few hundred words left of my thousand. I don't want to waste them, but I also don't want to stuff them full just to use them up. Silence is also a choice. White space matters.

So I'll leave you with this image, since it's what's coming to me now, unbidden:

Late evening. The sky not dark yet, but thinking about it. One star brave enough to go first. Someone opening a window to let the cool air in. Crickets doing their tiny, relentless work. And you, reading this, with 1000 words of your own somewhere inside you, waiting for someone — maybe just you — to say: go ahead. Write whatever comes.

I'll cup my hands around your spark if you cup yours around mine.
